fields.title: A/B: how long to wait and when not to look
fields.keyTakeaway: Sample size and duration are calculated before launch, based on the effect size you want to detect. Peeking and stopping at a convenient moment turns the experiment into a way to find randomness.
fields.checkQuestion: On the third day, variant B is ahead by 12%. Why shouldn't you stop the test?
fields.blocks/0/text: Continuation of the same question: **how the test itself is structured.** In the lesson on measuring change, we compared “before” and “after”; here a control group appears, and that is what gives the right to speak of causality.
fields.blocks/1/items/0: **Minimum detectable effect** — how small of a change you care about. The smaller it is, the larger the required sample.
fields.blocks/1/items/1: **Sample size** — follows from the first number and the current metric level. Calculated with a tool, not by eye.
fields.blocks/1/items/2: **Duration** — at least a full behavior cycle: if the scenario is weekly, three days will show nothing.
fields.blocks/2/text: If you check results every day and stop when the difference looks convincing, you are almost guaranteed to find an effect where there is none. Early days are the noisiest.
fields.blocks/3/subtitle: Testing your measurement system, not a hypothesis
fields.blocks/3/items/0: Both branches receive **the exact same thing**, and there should be no difference.
fields.blocks/3/items/1: If there is a difference, the split, tracking, or metric itself is broken.
fields.blocks/3/items/2: Cheap and one-off: A/A makes sense before the first serious experiment and after changes in analytics.
fields.blocks/4/text:
On the third day, the variant with a three-day trial was ahead by 12%. Rollout was suggested.

The card specified: four weeks, 22 thousand per branch. By the end of the second week, the gap shrank to 4%, and by the fourth week to 2.9%, against the stated target of 0.9 percentage points.

The early gap had a simple explanation: during the first days, weekend users who read more entered the branch. Had the test been stopped on the third day, a conclusion that was an artifact would have been rolled out to the entire base.
fields.blocks/4/title: Vetka: the test that was almost stopped
fields.blocks/5/text: A/B answers “what happened” and stays silent on why. It is unsuitable for rare events and small audiences: if an event occurs a hundred times a month, you will never detect a 10% change. And it only tests what is already built — before building, cheaper methods are needed.
